card.official_title: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Make higher income tax rates on high earners permanent
card.yes_means: The current higher income tax rates on high earners would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031. Revenue would continue to support schools, community colleges, other state programs and budget reserves.
card.no_means: The higher rates would remain temporary and expire in 2031 under current law. Affected high earners would then pay lower rates, and the state would stop collecting the revenue from those higher rates.
who_is_affected: High-income Californians who pay the higher rates
Public school and community college students and staff
People who rely on Medi-Cal and other state services
State and local school budget planners

fiscal_impact.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates that keeping the higher rates after their scheduled expiration would maintain $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue. The amount would vary widely with the economy and stock market.
fiscal_impact.label: fact

steelman_yes.core_claim: This common-sense measure will definitely protect every classroom from devastating cuts, so voters should vote yes.

best_evidence.text: The higher rates apply to the top 2 percent of taxpayers, rather than taxpayers generally.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Supporters warn that allowing the rates to expire could lead to teacher layoffs, larger classes and reduced access to health care.
best_evidence.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The official summary says local school boards decide how school revenue is spent and bars its use for administrative costs.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Supporters point to students, educators, families using health services and communities that depend on state-funded programs.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters argue that this keeps current rates rather than raising them today. They say the school funding protections address accountability, while allowing the tax to expire would put essential services at risk.

steelman_no.core_claim: Opponents are wealthy people who just don't want to pay their fair share.

best_evidence.text: The measure removes the scheduled expiration of higher rates that voters first approved as temporary in 2012.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Opponents point to taxpayers who would otherwise keep paying higher rates and Californians who want tighter control over state spending.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: They have no real answer; they just want lower taxes.

crux.text: Should California keep a major source of funding for services, or honor the scheduled end of a temporary tax? The sides also disagree about whether spending reforms could protect services without this revenue.

evidence.text: The measure keeps current higher rates; it does not raise them today. Compared with current law after their scheduled expiration in 2031, it keeps taxes higher for affected earners.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: At 2025 income levels, the higher rates apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers, $742,000 for joint filers and $505,000 for heads of household. These thresholds adjust annually for inflation.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would support other state programs, with some set aside in reserves.
evidence.label: prediction

evidence.text: Permanent tax rates would not guarantee a steady revenue amount. The Legislative Analyst expects large yearly swings because much of the taxed income is tied to the stock market.
evidence.label: prediction
